course.title: SQL Masterclass
course.tagline: Zero to advanced, one module at a time.
course.standard: PostgreSQL-first, with MySQL, SQLite and SQL Server notes.
course.description: Module 14 teaches string concatenation, trimming, slicing, replacement, string aggregation, date and time types, date arithmetic, numeric functions and casts.
outcomes: Cast between types without hiding errors

modules.title: String, Date and Numeric Functions
modules.goal: Transform text, dates and numbers correctly at query time.

topics.title: Introduction to SQL Functions
topics.simple: SQL functions values ko transform karte hain.
topics.pro: Functions take input values and return a computed value; string, date and numeric functions let you clean, format and calculate without changing stored data.
points: Functions do not modify the table.
They can be used in SELECT, WHERE and ORDER BY.
NULL input often produces NULL output.

example.sql: SELECT UPPER(name) AS shout FROM students;

topics.title: String Concatenation
topics.simple: || aur CONCAT strings ko jodte hain.
topics.pro: The || operator concatenates strings and propagates NULL, while CONCAT ignores NULL arguments and CONCAT_WS joins only non-null values with a separator.

example.sql: SELECT name || ' (' || COALESCE(email, 'none') || ')' AS label FROM students;
example.output: A label with a visible fallback.

topics.title: LENGTH and CHAR_LENGTH
topics.simple: LENGTH string ke characters ginata hai.
topics.pro: LENGTH and CHAR_LENGTH return the number of characters in a string; OCTET_LENGTH counts bytes and BIT_LENGTH counts bits.

example.sql: SELECT name, LENGTH(name) AS chars FROM students;
example.output: Each name with its character count.

topics.title: UPPER and LOWER
topics.simple: UPPER uppercase aur LOWER lowercase karta hai.
topics.pro: UPPER and LOWER change letter case using the database collation, which is useful for display and case-insensitive comparisons.
points: They do not change stored data.

example.sql: SELECT UPPER(name) AS uppercase, LOWER(name) AS lowercase FROM students;

topics.title: TRIM, LTRIM and RTRIM
topics.simple: TRIM whitespace ya chosen characters hataata hai.
topics.pro: TRIM removes leading and trailing characters, LTRIM only leading and RTRIM only trailing; BTRIM is the explicit both-sides function.
points: You can specify the character set.
It does not remove inner spaces.

example.sql: SELECT TRIM('  Aarav  ') AS cleaned;

topics.title: SUBSTRING
topics.simple: SUBSTRING string ka slice nikaalta hai.
topics.pro: SUBSTRING(text FROM start FOR length) returns a one-indexed slice; a missing length returns the rest of the string.
points: Out-of-range slices return available characters or empty.

example.sql: SELECT SUBSTRING(name FROM 1 FOR 3) AS short FROM students;

topics.title: REPLACE
topics.simple: REPLACE matching text ko naye text se badalta hai.
topics.pro: REPLACE(text, from, to) replaces every occurrence of a substring and returns the original when no match exists.

example.sql: SELECT REPLACE(email, '@example.com', '@school.edu') AS school_email FROM students;

topics.title: POSITION and STRPOS
topics.simple: POSITION substring ka index batata hai.
topics.pro: POSITION(sub IN text) and STRPOS(text, sub) return the one-indexed position of the first match, or 0 when absent.

example.sql: SELECT name, POSITION('a' IN name) AS first_a FROM students;

topics.title: LEFT, RIGHT, LPAD and RPAD
topics.simple: LEFT/RIGHT slice karte hain; LPAD/RPAD padding add karte hain.
topics.pro: LEFT and RIGHT return a prefix or suffix, while LPAD and RPAD pad a string to a target length with a fill string.
points: LPAD/RPAD can truncate if the target is shorter.
Padding is useful for fixed-width codes.

example.sql: SELECT LEFT(name, 3) AS prefix, LPAD(id::text, 5, '0') AS padded_id FROM students;
example.output: A prefix and a zero-padded id.

topics.title: STRING_AGG and ARRAY_AGG
topics.simple: STRING_AGG values ko ek string me jodta hai; ARRAY_AGG array banata hai.
topics.pro: STRING_AGG concatenates values per group with a separator and optional ORDER BY, while ARRAY_AGG collects them into an array.
points: ORDER BY inside controls the order.

example.sql: SELECT s.name, STRING_AGG(c.title, ', ' ORDER BY c.title) AS courses FROM students s JOIN enrollments e ON e.student_id = s.id JOIN courses c ON c.id = e.course_id GROUP BY s.id, s.name;
example.output: One comma-separated course list per student.

topics.title: Date and Time Types
topics.simple: DATE, TIME, TIMESTAMP aur INTERVAL alag concepts hain.
topics.pro: DATE stores a calendar date, TIME stores a time of day, TIMESTAMP stores date and time, TIMESTAMPTZ stores an instant with time zone, and INTERVAL stores a duration.

example.sql: SELECT enrolled_on, enrolled_on::timestamp AS at_midnight FROM enrollments;
example.output: A date and its timestamp form.

topics.title: Current Date and Time
topics.simple: CURRENT_DATE aur CURRENT_TIMESTAMP current values dete hain.
topics.pro: CURRENT_DATE returns the session date, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP and NOW() return the transaction start time, and CURRENT_TIME returns the time of day.

example.sql: SELECT CURRENT_DATE AS today, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP AS now;
example.output: The session date and transaction timestamp.

topics.title: EXTRACT
topics.simple: EXTRACT date ke part ko number me nikaalta hai.
topics.pro: EXTRACT(field FROM timestamp) returns a numeric component such as year, month, day, hour or epoch.

example.sql: SELECT EXTRACT(YEAR FROM enrolled_on) AS year, EXTRACT(MONTH FROM enrolled_on) AS month FROM enrollments;

topics.title: DATE_TRUNC
topics.simple: DATE_TRUNC date ko chosen unit ke start par le aata hai.
topics.pro: DATE_TRUNC('unit', value) truncates a timestamp to the beginning of the unit, which is the standard way to group by month, week or year.
points: Units include day, week, month, quarter and year.
It is ideal for GROUP BY.

example.sql: SELECT DATE_TRUNC('month', enrolled_on) AS month, COUNT(*) AS total FROM enrollments GROUP BY month ORDER BY month;

topics.title: Date Arithmetic and Intervals
topics.simple: Dates aur intervals ko add/subtract kar sakte hain.
topics.pro: Date arithmetic adds or subtracts INTERVAL values, while subtracting two dates yields an integer day count and subtracting timestamps yields an interval.

example.sql: SELECT enrolled_on, enrolled_on + INTERVAL '30 days' AS due_on FROM enrollments;
example.output: A due date thirty days later.

topics.title: AGE and Duration
topics.simple: AGE do timestamps ka human-readable difference deta hai.
topics.pro: AGE(later, earlier) returns an interval broken into years, months and days, while AGE(timestamp) compares against the current date.
points: It is useful for tenure and age.

example.sql: SELECT AGE(DATE '2026-01-15', DATE '2025-01-15') AS duration;

topics.title: ROUND, CEIL, FLOOR and TRUNC
topics.simple: Rounding functions decimal ko nearest, up, down ya cut karte hain.
topics.pro: ROUND rounds to a scale, CEIL rounds up, FLOOR rounds down and TRUNC cuts toward zero without rounding.

example.sql: SELECT ROUND(7.0 / 2, 1) AS rounded, CEIL(4.2) AS up, FLOOR(4.8) AS down, TRUNC(4.8) AS cut;

topics.title: ABS, MOD, POWER and SQRT
topics.simple: Numeric helpers absolute value, remainder, power aur root dete hain.
topics.pro: ABS returns magnitude, MOD returns the remainder, POWER raises a number and SQRT returns the square root.
points: SQRT of a negative is an error.

example.sql: SELECT ABS(-5) AS distance, MOD(10, 3) AS remainder, POWER(2, 3) AS cubed, SQRT(16) AS root;

topics.title: CAST and Type Conversion
topics.simple: CAST value ko doosre type me badalta hai.
topics.pro: CAST(value AS type) and the :: shorthand convert between compatible types; invalid text raises an error rather than silently becoming NULL.

example.sql: SELECT CAST('42' AS INTEGER) AS number, '2026-01-15'::date AS day;

topics.title: Practical Reporting with Functions
topics.simple: Ab text, date aur numeric functions ko report me combine karo.
topics.pro: A practical report cleans text, formats dates, rounds numbers and handles NULL explicitly so the output is stable and readable.

example.sql: SELECT UPPER(LEFT(TRIM(s.name), 1)) || LOWER(SUBSTRING(TRIM(s.name) FROM 2)) AS display_name, TO_CHAR(MIN(e.enrolled_on), 'DD Mon YYYY') AS first_enrolled, ROUND(AVG(s.marks), 2) AS average_marks FROM students s LEFT JOIN enrollments e ON e.student_id = s.id GROUP BY s.id, s.name ORDER BY s.name;

learn.q: Which function ignores NULL arguments when concatenating?
learn.why: CONCAT treats NULL as empty in PostgreSQL.
OCTET_LENGTH and BIT_LENGTH count bytes and bits.
It changes letter case for the result.

learn.q: What does TRIM remove by default?
learn.why: TRIM removes leading and trailing spaces by default.

learn.q: What is the first character position in SUBSTRING?
learn.why: SQL string positions are one-indexed.

learn.answer: Replaces every occurrence of a substring
learn.why: All matching occurrences are replaced.

learn.q: What does POSITION return when there is no match?
learn.why: No match is reported as position 0.
LEFT takes a prefix.

options: Joins values into one string per group
learn.answer: Joins values into one string per group
learn.why: It concatenates values with a separator.

learn.q: Which type stores a calendar date without time?
learn.why: DATE has no time component.
It is stable within a transaction.
It extracts a field such as year or month.

learn.answer: Truncates to the start of a unit
learn.why: It is used to group by month, week or year.
PostgreSQL subtracts dates to days.
It expresses a calendar difference.
CEIL rounds up.
FLOOR rounds down.
It is the remainder.

learn.why: Invalid input syntax is an error.

interview.q: What is the difference between || and CONCAT?
interview.answer: || returns NULL if any operand is NULL; CONCAT ignores NULL arguments.

interview.q: What does LENGTH count?
interview.answer: Characters, not bytes.

interview.q: How do you make a case-insensitive comparison?
interview.answer: Compare LOWER(column) to LOWER(value), or use a case-insensitive collation.

interview.q: How do you remove both leading and trailing spaces?
interview.answer: Use TRIM(text).

interview.q: How do you extract the first three characters?
interview.answer: Use LEFT(text, 3) or SUBSTRING(text FROM 1 FOR 3).

interview.q: How do you replace part of a string?
interview.answer: Use REPLACE(text, from, to).

interview.q: How do you find a substring position?
interview.answer: Use POSITION(sub IN text) or STRPOS(text, sub).

interview.q: How do you concatenate values per group?
interview.answer: Use STRING_AGG(column, separator ORDER BY ...) with GROUP BY.

interview.q: What is the difference between DATE and TIMESTAMP?
interview.answer: DATE stores only a calendar date; TIMESTAMP stores date and time.

interview.q: What is TIMESTAMPTZ?
interview.answer: A timestamp with time zone that stores an instant.

interview.q: What is the difference between NOW() and CURRENT_DATE?
interview.answer: NOW() returns the transaction start timestamp; CURRENT_DATE returns the session date.

interview.q: How do you get the year from a date?
interview.answer: Use EXTRACT(YEAR FROM date).

interview.q: How do you group by month?
interview.answer: Use DATE_TRUNC('month', date_column) in GROUP BY.

interview.q: How do you add thirty days to a date?
interview.answer: Use date + INTERVAL '30 days'.

interview.q: What does timestamp subtraction return?
interview.answer: An interval.

interview.q: How do you calculate age or tenure?
interview.answer: Use AGE(later, earlier) or subtract the dates.

interview.q: What is the difference between ROUND and TRUNC?
interview.answer: ROUND changes the value to the nearest scale; TRUNC cuts digits without rounding.

interview.q: What does CEIL do?
interview.answer: Rounds up to the next integer or scale.

interview.q: How do you convert text to an integer?
interview.answer: Use CAST(text AS INTEGER) or text::integer.

interview.q: How do you format a date for display?
interview.answer: Use TO_CHAR(date, 'YYYY-MM-DD') or another format pattern.

labs.title: Concatenate with fallback
labs.task: Build a name and email label, showing none for missing email.
labs.solution: SELECT name || ' (' || COALESCE(email, 'none') || ')' AS label FROM students;

labs.title: Length
labs.task: Return each name with its character count.
labs.solution: SELECT name, LENGTH(name) AS chars FROM students;

labs.title: Case conversion
labs.task: Return each name in uppercase and lowercase.
labs.solution: SELECT UPPER(name) AS uppercase, LOWER(name) AS lowercase FROM students;

labs.title: Trim
labs.task: Remove surrounding spaces from a literal.
labs.solution: SELECT TRIM('  Aarav  ') AS cleaned;

labs.title: Substring
labs.task: Return the first three characters of each name.
labs.solution: SELECT SUBSTRING(name FROM 1 FOR 3) AS short FROM students;

labs.title: Replace
labs.task: Rewrite example.com emails to school.edu.
labs.solution: SELECT REPLACE(email, '@example.com', '@school.edu') AS school_email FROM students;

labs.title: Position
labs.task: Return the first lowercase-a position in each name.
labs.solution: SELECT name, POSITION('a' IN name) AS first_a FROM students;

labs.title: Left and pad
labs.task: Return a three-character prefix and a zero-padded id.
labs.solution: SELECT LEFT(name, 3) AS prefix, LPAD(id::text, 5, '0') AS padded_id FROM students;

labs.title: String aggregate
labs.task: Return a comma-separated course list per student.
labs.solution: SELECT s.name, STRING_AGG(c.title, ', ' ORDER BY c.title) AS courses FROM students s JOIN enrollments e ON e.student_id = s.id JOIN courses c ON c.id = e.course_id GROUP BY s.id, s.name;

labs.title: Date parts
labs.task: Return the year and month of each enrollment.
labs.solution: SELECT EXTRACT(YEAR FROM enrolled_on) AS year, EXTRACT(MONTH FROM enrolled_on) AS month FROM enrollments;

labs.title: Monthly grouping
labs.task: Count enrollments by month.
labs.solution: SELECT DATE_TRUNC('month', enrolled_on) AS month, COUNT(*) AS total FROM enrollments GROUP BY month ORDER BY month;

labs.title: Date arithmetic
labs.task: Return a due date thirty days after enrollment.
labs.solution: SELECT enrolled_on, enrolled_on + INTERVAL '30 days' AS due_on FROM enrollments;

labs.title: Age
labs.task: Return the calendar difference between two dates.
labs.solution: SELECT AGE(DATE '2026-01-15', DATE '2025-01-15') AS duration;

labs.title: Rounding
labs.task: Round 3.5, round up 4.2, round down 4.8 and truncate 4.8.
labs.solution: SELECT ROUND(7.0 / 2, 1) AS rounded, CEIL(4.2) AS up, FLOOR(4.8) AS down, TRUNC(4.8) AS cut;

labs.title: Numeric helpers
labs.task: Return absolute value, remainder, power and square root.
labs.solution: SELECT ABS(-5) AS distance, MOD(10, 3) AS remainder, POWER(2, 3) AS cubed, SQRT(16) AS root;

labs.title: Cast text to number
labs.task: Convert the text 42 to an integer and a date string to date.
labs.solution: SELECT CAST('42' AS INTEGER) AS number, '2026-01-15'::date AS day;

labs.title: Format a date
labs.task: Format the current date as DD Mon YYYY.
labs.solution: SELECT TO_CHAR(CURRENT_DATE, 'DD Mon YYYY') AS formatted;

labs.title: Split a string
labs.task: Return the second comma-separated part of a,b,c.
labs.solution: SELECT SPLIT_PART('a,b,c', ',', 2) AS second;

labs.title: Initcap
labs.task: Capitalize each word in a name.
labs.solution: SELECT INITCAP('aarav sharma') AS display_name;

labs.title: Formatted report
labs.task: Build a formatted student report.
labs.solution: SELECT UPPER(LEFT(TRIM(s.name), 1)) || LOWER(SUBSTRING(TRIM(s.name) FROM 2)) AS display_name, TO_CHAR(MIN(e.enrolled_on), 'DD Mon YYYY') AS first_enrolled, ROUND(AVG(s.marks), 2) AS average_marks FROM students s LEFT JOIN enrollments e ON e.student_id = s.id GROUP BY s.id, s.name ORDER BY s.name;

logic.q: Why does || return NULL when one side is NULL?
logic.answer: NULL means unknown, so the concatenated result is unknown rather than partially known.

logic.q: Why is CONCAT useful for labels?
logic.answer: It ignores NULL arguments, so a missing field does not erase the whole label.
It gives a readable fallback and keeps the result non-null.

logic.q: Why can LOWER comparisons be slow?
logic.answer: A function on the column can prevent a plain index from being used; a functional or case-insensitive index may be needed.

logic.q: Why are SQL string positions one-indexed?
logic.answer: SQL follows a one-based convention for string positions.
It maps every date in a month to the same timestamp, producing one group per month.

logic.q: Why is NOW() stable inside a transaction?
logic.answer: It returns the transaction start time, so multiple calls agree.

logic.q: Why does date subtraction return days?
logic.answer: PostgreSQL defines date minus date as an integer day difference.

logic.q: Why is timestamp subtraction an interval?
logic.answer: Timestamps have time-of-day precision, so the difference is a duration.

logic.q: Why use INTERVAL instead of adding 30?
logic.answer: Adding an integer to a date adds days, but INTERVAL makes the unit explicit and supports months, hours and minutes.

logic.q: Why can ROUND behave differently on double precision?
logic.answer: PostgreSQL’s two-argument ROUND requires numeric, so a double may need an explicit cast.

logic.q: Why is TRUNC different from ROUND?
logic.answer: TRUNC cuts digits; ROUND changes the value based on the next digit.

logic.q: Why can SQRT of a negative fail?
logic.answer: The square root of a negative real number is not defined in this numeric context.

logic.q: Why does CAST fail instead of returning NULL?
logic.answer: Invalid input is an error; silently returning NULL would hide bad data.

logic.q: Why format dates at the presentation layer?
logic.answer: Stored dates should stay typed; display formatting belongs in the report or UI.
